practices.name: Operational Excellence Practice
practices.description: A methodology dedicated to reducing production issues by institutionalizing a DevOps culture, formalizing Safe Deployment Practices (SDP), and establishing holistic, AI-enhanced system observability to ensure repeatable and reliable workload operations.

narratives.name: DevOps and Observability
narratives.description: The necessity of standardized workflows, rigorous automation, and cultural alignment.

narrativeContexts.context: To maintain high workload quality at velocity, traditional silos between engineering and operations teams must be dismantled. Organizations must embrace a shared responsibility model where developers own the operational health of their code.

Operational Excellence dictates the relentless automation of repetitive tasks. By utilizing Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and robust CI/CD pipelines, teams guarantee safe, incremental, and highly predictable deployments, severely limiting the blast radius of human error.

Furthermore, generating actionable telemetry—distinguishing properly between metrics, logs, and traces—allows teams to shift from reactive firefighting to proactive health modeling. As maturity increases, this telemetry feeds into AI-driven automation to intelligently optimize runtime configurations without manual intervention.

alphas.name: DevOps Culture

practices.name: Performance Efficiency Practice
practices.description: A methodology ensuring workloads adapt efficiently to dynamic demands via continuous capacity planning, optimizing horizontal scaling strategies, and fine-tuning application code and data usage.

narratives.name: Scaling Dynamics
narratives.description: The core premise of performance optimization in distributed cloud systems.

narrativeContexts.context: Cloud architectures offer nearly limitless scale, but utilizing brute-force overprovisioning to handle load destroys the economic ROI of the platform.

True performance efficiency demands rigorous, predictive capacity planning, sophisticated horizontal scaling configurations, and the continuous profiling of code to ensure the system gracefully handles sudden traffic spikes without incurring unnecessary resource consumption.
By formalizing performance metrics into automated quality gates, engineering teams prevent performance regressions from ever reaching the production environment.

alphas.name: Performance Targets
alphas.description: The measurable capacity, throughput, and latency requirements the system must fulfill under varying loads.

states.name: Conceived
states.description: High-level performance expectations and baseline traffic estimates are stated (Maturity Level 1).

checklist.name: Expectations Listed
checklist.description: Basic load expectations and acceptable user experience thresholds are documented

states.name: Bounded
states.description: Specific numerical targets are defined based on predictive capacity planning and logical modeling (Maturity Level 2).

checklist.name: Targets Quantified
checklist.description: Explicit latency and throughput targets (e.g., sub-200ms response) are set for all critical flows

checklist.name: Capacity Modeled
checklist.description: Predictive models forecast future demand based on business events and historical usage patterns

states.name: Addressed
states.description: Scalability solutions are contextualized, and the system is rigorously load-tested (Maturity Level 3).

checklist.name: Load Tested
checklist.description: The system undergoes active load testing in production-like environments using synthetic traffic

checklist.name: Scaling Validated
checklist.description: Horizontal scaling responds appropriately to simulated spikes without causing database contention

states.name: Fulfilled
states.description: Automated scaling rules and continuous code profiling are actively optimizing production (Maturity Level 4).

checklist.name: Auto-Scaling Active
checklist.description: Automated horizontal scaling rules trigger reliably based on live telemetry

checklist.name: Continuous Profiling
checklist.description: Telemetry continuously profiles code efficiency, identifying degradation over time

workProducts.name: Capacity Plan

checklist.name: Hardware Listed
checklist.description: High-level lists of required compute nodes and data stores are drafted

levelsOfDetail.description: Detailed sizing logic, partitioning rules, and multi-region scale unit designs (Maturity Level 2).

checklist.name: Logic Documented
checklist.description: Sizing logic correlates directly with user growth projections and specific service quotas

levelsOfDetail.name: Automated
levelsOfDetail.description: Automated capacity planning calculators linked to live telemetry dashboards (Maturity Level 4).

checklist.name: Auto-Calculators Active
checklist.description: Capacity plans update automatically based on real-time telemetry trends, adjusting forecasts dynamically

activities.name: Conduct Capacity Planning
activities.description: The process of forecasting future demand, establishing performance targets, and defining the scale unit architecture to meet it.

personas.name: Performance Engineer
personas.description: A specialist dedicated to executing complex load testing, deep code profiling, and architecting highly elastic scaling units.

personaGroups.name: Performance Team
personaGroups.description: The cross-functional group responsible for ensuring the system remains highly responsive under severe, variable load.

patterns.name: Load Spike Resolution
patterns.description: A STAR narrative pattern demonstrating the practical application of performance efficiency to resolve severe operational degradation.

patternViews.name: Situation
patternViews.description: The system encounters unexpected, catastrophic scaling limits.

narrativeContexts.context: During a major seasonal retail event, concurrent user traffic spiked by 400% within minutes. This sudden load overwhelmed the static database tier, causing connection pool exhaustion and severe latency degradation across critical checkout flows.

patternViews.name: Task
patternViews.description: Identifying the performance bottleneck and formulating an immediate remediation plan.

narrativeContexts.context: The objective was to immediately identify the core bottleneck, decouple the read/write paths to relieve database pressure, and implement dynamic horizontal scaling without interrupting live transactional processing.

patternViews.name: Action
patternViews.description: Applying scaling logic, capacity planning, and architectural optimization.

narrativeContexts.context: The performance team implemented an aggressive read-replica caching layer using an in-memory datastore.
Simultaneously, they refactored the compute scale units to trigger auto-scaling based on custom telemetry (specifically request queue depth) rather than lagging, raw CPU utilization metrics.

patternViews.name: Result
patternViews.description: The system reaches an automated, fulfilled state of performance efficiency.

narrativeContexts.context: Average response times returned to strict sub-200ms levels.
The newly architected, queue-driven scaling successfully absorbed subsequent traffic spikes dynamically, optimizing resource usage in real-time and ultimately lowering peak compute costs by 30%.

practices.name: Well-Architected Assessment Practice
practices.description: A centralized, coordinating lifecycle practice that governs the continuous evaluation, scoring, and methodical remediation of cloud workloads against the five foundational pillars of architectural excellence.

narratives.name: Continuous Review Strategy
narratives.description: The operational mechanics and strategic importance of continuously assessing workloads.

narrativeContexts.context: A well-architected design is never a static achievement. As business demands pivot, feature velocity increases, and minor technical debt accrues sprint over sprint, workloads inevitably drift from their initially optimized state.
To combat this entropy, the Azure Well-Architected Review provides a formalized mechanism—a structured, multi-dimensional assessment—to objectively quantify workload maturity across all five pillars.

This practice institutionalizes the assessment process, ensuring that exporting remediation recommendations into the SDLC backlog becomes a routine, automated facet of engineering governance, guaranteeing continuous architectural improvement.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature. It avoids the generic term **the user** to provide context on their technical ability, permissions, and needs.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I wan to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the **what,** not the **how.** Avoid mentioning specific UI elements like **click a red button.** Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you can’t find a compelling **So that** statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a "north star" for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value (e.g., "Increasing retention by 10%"), it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: "Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic?" If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as "themes" to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the "Definition of Done" for the entire project. Instead of saying "when the code is finished," use "when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%."

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: Citation Standard
narrativeTypes.description: The structural elements required for a reference list entry.

narrativeElements.name: Author
narrativeElements.description: The person, group, or organization responsible for the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Invert authors' names (Lastname, F. M.). Use an ampersand (&) before the final author's name in a list. For groups, use the full name.

narrativeElements.name: Date
narrativeElements.description: The publication date of the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Enclose the year in parentheses, followed by a period: (2026). For works with no date, use (n.d.).

narrativeElements.name: Title
narrativeElements.description: The name of the specific work being cited.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Italicize the title of standalone works (books, reports). Use sentence case—capitalize only the first word of the title and subtitle.

narrativeElements.name: Source
narrativeElements.description: Where the work can be retrieved, such as a journal, publisher, or URL.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Include the periodical title and volume/issue if applicable. Provide a DOI or URL as a live link; do not include 'Retrieved from' for most entries.

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise IT managers face hurdles such as operational complexity and security risks when managing siloed tools across multiple cloud providers.
Red Hat OpenShift provides a unified platform to standardize workloads, boosting efficiency through CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, and automated provisioning.
By moving through the OEAM, organizations achieve faster releases, improved service delivery, and optimized costs through granular resource allocation.

narratives.name: The Mind-Shift Challenge
narratives.description: The organizational and cultural shift required for successful platform adoption.

narrativeContexts.context: Adopting OpenShift Virtualization requires a significant mental shift for teams familiar with traditional virtualization tooling.
Success depends on executive buy-in and the structural integration of Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) teams into a single collaborative unit.
The learning curve is mitigated by well-developed migration toolkits and close support from technical experts.

name: Community Cloud-Native IDP
description: A unified, socio-technical methodology designed to replicate the cohesive, frictionless developer experience of Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) using upstream Kubernetes components. The Method orchestrates the transition from traditional, siloed IT operations to a product-centric platform engineering paradigm, delivering automated lifecycle management, secure-by-default guardrails, and self-service Golden Paths. By decoupling the underlying infrastructure from the developer interface, the Method enables hyper-customization.

activitySpaces.name: Explore Possibilities
activitySpaces.description: Explore the possibilities presented by the creation of a new or improved platform.

activitySpaces.name: Assess Business Value
activitySpaces.description: Conduct rigorous business analysis to quantify potential ROI, map platform capabilities to organizational value streams, and secure executive sponsorship.

activitySpaces.name: Monitor Value Realization
activitySpaces.description: Track KPIs such as deployment frequency, MTTR, and developer adoption rates to proactively manage bottlenecks and prove continuous ROI.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Platform Economics
activitySpaces.description: Define chargeback/showback models, right-size infrastructure, optimize costs through FinOps practices, and transition from CapEx to OpEx.

activitySpaces.name: Engage Platform Consumers
activitySpaces.description: Conduct user research, utilize Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks, and ensure the platform demonstrates value through product management practices.

activitySpaces.name: Evangelize and Support
activitySpaces.description: Provide internal marketing, create feedback loops, and deliver accessible support to ensure continuous voluntary adoption by stream-aligned teams.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Secure Guardrails
activitySpaces.description: Shift security left, embed Zero Trust principles, and codify compliance requirements into automated scanning tools to ensure secure-by-default platform operations.

activitySpaces.name: Define Platform Capabilities
activitySpaces.description: Distill stakeholder feedback into actionable requirements and define the Thinnest Viable Platform (TVP) to avoid over-engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Architect and Build the Foundation
activitySpaces.description: Establish declarative provisioning (IaC), build CI/CD pipelines, configure connectivity, deploy orchestration engines, and instantiate the six pillars of platform engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Operate and Evolve the System
activitySpaces.description: Execute Day-2 operations using SRE practices, manage observability telemetry, ensure high availability, and continuously evolve the platform.

activitySpaces.name: Develop the Golden Paths
activitySpaces.description: Build Internal Developer Portals (IDPs), intuitive CLIs, and automated scaffolding templates to drastically reduce cognitive load and enable autonomous self-service.

activitySpaces.name: Integrate Toolchain Services
activitySpaces.description: Specify, acquire, and securely integrate individual platform assets ensuring seamless interoperability with established Golden Paths.

activitySpaces.name: Prepare To Do The Work
activitySpaces.description: Prepare to do the work required for the platform.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Work Execution
activitySpaces.description: Manage agile delivery cycles, allocate engineering capacity, and track velocity to ensure predictable platform feature development.

activitySpaces.name: Structure Organizational Topologies
activitySpaces.description: Define clear team interaction modes, establish X-as-a-Service boundaries, and continuously assess cognitive load using Team Topologies principles.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Operational Practices
activitySpaces.description: Define incident response procedures, institute blameless post-mortems, standardize CI methodologies, and foster a continuous-learning culture.

activitySpaces.name: Implement Policy-as-Code
activitySpaces.description: Translate manual governance rules into automated, machine-readable policies that execute within deployment pipelines without impeding velocity.

activitySpaces.name: Drive Cultural Transformation
activitySpaces.description: Execute formal change management programs, upskill engineering talent, address behavioral resistance, and facilitate the shift to product-driven platform engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Stop The Work
activitySpaces.description: Stop the work and close out the endeavor.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure & StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature. It avoids the generic term **the user** to provide context on their technical ability, permissions, and needs.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I wan to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the **what,** not the **how.** Avoid mentioning specific UI elements like **click a red button.** Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you can’t find a compelling **So that** statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a "north star" for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value (e.g., "Increasing retention by 10%"), it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: "Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic?" If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as "themes" to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the "Definition of Done" for the entire project. Instead of saying "when the code is finished," use "when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%."

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: Citation Standard
narrativeTypes.description: The structural elements required for a reference list entry.

narrativeElements.name: Author
narrativeElements.description: The person, group, or organization responsible for the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Invert authors' names (Lastname, F. M.). Use an ampersand (&) before the final author's name in a list. For groups, use the full name.

narrativeElements.name: Date
narrativeElements.description: The publication date of the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Enclose the year in parentheses, followed by a period: (2026). For works with no date, use (n.d.).

narrativeElements.name: Title
narrativeElements.description: The name of the specific work being cited.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Italicize the title of standalone works (books, reports). Use sentence case—capitalize only the first word of the title and subtitle.

narrativeElements.name: Source
narrativeElements.description: Where the work can be retrieved, such as a journal, publisher, or URL.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Include the periodical title and volume/issue if applicable. Provide a DOI or URL as a live link; do not include 'Retrieved from' for most entries.

practices.name: Platform Foundation Architecture Practice
practices.description: This practice governs the foundational construction of the Internal Developer Platform. It focuses on the rigorous selection of upstream CNCF components, the configuration of advanced multi-cluster networking capabilities, and the critical restructuring of traditional infrastructure teams into a unified, product-centric platform organization.

narratives.name: Foundational IDP Architecture
narratives.description: The overarching context for transitioning foundational infrastructure to standard CNCF abstractions.

narrativeContexts.context: Historically, infrastructure and operations organizations operated in technology-aligned silos, maintaining distinct teams for compute, networking, and continuous delivery. This outdated structure generates massive friction, requiring application developers to file multiple asynchronous tickets across different departments simply to deploy a standard microservice.

To successfully build, maintain, and scale an effective IDP, the organization must adopt a cross-functional model based on the principles of Team Topologies, focusing entirely on the end-to-end developer experience and effectively operating as an internal product company serving captive enterprise customers.

Technologically, this transition demands the replacement of legacy ingress controllers and proprietary routing logic with the highly portable, expressive, and extensible Kubernetes Gateway API. This role-oriented design cleanly separates the responsibilities of infrastructure providers, cluster operators, and application developers.

Ultimately, the platform must adhere strictly to standard orchestration interfaces and Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs), ensuring deep ecosystem interoperability, the prevention of tool sprawl, and true operational portability across disparate cloud environments.

narratives.name: The Dissolution of Silos
narratives.description: The rationale for moving away from technology-aligned operational teams.

narrativeContexts.context: A technically flawless Kubernetes architecture will inevitably fail to deliver value if the organizational structure responsible for maintaining it is misaligned.

Historically, operations organizations maintained distinct teams for compute, networking, and CI/CD. This outdated structure generates massive friction, requiring developers to navigate convoluted approval processes across different departments.
The primary reason internal platforms fail is not due to technological inadequacy, but rather organizing the platform around technology stacks instead of user needs.

To effectively scale the IDP, the organization must adopt a cross-functional model, effectively operating as an internal product company serving captive enterprise customers through cohesive, interdisciplinary units.

narratives.name: Component Selection Strategy
narratives.description: The framework and criteria utilized for selecting foundational platform components.

narrativeContexts.context: The selection process for building an internal developer platform from the CNCF ecosystem is a highly complex architectural exercise requiring rigorous evaluation criteria to prevent tooling sprawl and fragmented operational states.

Components must be evaluated primarily on composability and loose coupling, allowing product teams to consume only the specific capabilities they explicitly need while gracefully falling back to standard Kubernetes primitives if abstractions prove inadequate.

Tools must rely on standard Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions rather than proprietary sidecars, closed-source agents, or non-standard APIs that introduce deep vendor lock-in and compromise operational portability.

Furthermore, chosen projects must possess deep, API-level integration symmetry to ensure the platform operates as a cohesive unit. For instance, ensuring that GitOps controllers natively understand the Custom Resources generated by the multicluster management engines.

practices.name: Platform Governance & Security Practice
practices.description: This practice establishes the automated guardrails, dynamic compliance validation, and integrated observability required to secure the IDP. It focuses heavily on implementing dynamic admission controllers and policy-as-code to enforce enterprise standards securely by default, effectively replacing static, manual compliance checks with proactive, system-enforced governance.

narratives.name: Enterprise Governance and Security
narratives.description: How the IDP replaces manual compliance with proactive automation and immutability.

narrativeContexts.context: A critical value proposition of a mature, enterprise-grade platform is its secure-by-default posture, traditionally enforced by proprietary Security Context Constraints (SCC).

With upstream Kubernetes deprecating basic Pod Security Policies in favor of highly basic admission controllers, relying solely on default RBAC leaves significant governance gaps for enterprise workloads handling sensitive data.

To provide equivalent or superior guardrails, organizations must implement advanced dynamic admission controllers that actively intercept, validate, mutate, and generate Kubernetes resources in real-time.

Furthermore, maintaining this secure posture requires autonomous dependency management systems that continuously scan internal repositories and automatically generate pull requests for critical security flaws across the vast ecosystem of CNCF projects.

practices.name: Golden Path Consumption Practice
practices.description: This practice defines exactly how application developers interact with the IDP to extract value. It covers the creation of opinionated project scaffolding, the abstraction of Dockerfiles via Enterprise Build Strategies (Shipwright/Buildpacks), and the GitOps workflows utilized to deploy microservices rapidly and securely.

narratives.name: The Paved Road Experience
narratives.description: The operational philosophy of how developers consume platform services frictionlessly.

narrativeContexts.context: The primary technological output of the platform engineering organization is the design and implementation of Golden Paths—highly opinionated, fully automated routes for executing common developer tasks.

The underlying philosophy is simple: if application developers choose to stay on the established Golden Path, they are guaranteed a frictionless, highly secure, and fully supported route to production without needing to understand intricate Kubernetes mechanics or complex network routing configurations.

Constructing a robust Golden Path encompasses project templating through intelligent scaffolding engines, automated CI/CD provisioning, inherently baked-in observability, and policy-as-code guardrails.

By deeply focusing on developer psychology and providing a fundamentally safe, zero-configuration method to ship code, the platform team effectively eliminates cognitive load. This confidence directly leads to faster iterations, drastically lower risks of misconfiguration, and a dramatic acceleration in overall organizational delivery velocity as proven by DORA metrics.

patternViews.name: Developer Cognitive Load Situation
patternViews.description: The developer needs to deploy a complex service but faces massive cognitive load attempting to craft manual Dockerfiles and complex ingress YAML.

narrativeContexts.context: An application developer is tasked with creating a new Java microservice but lacks deep, specialized expertise in writing highly optimized, multi-stage Dockerfiles or managing low-level Kubernetes ingress configurations securely.

Historically, in a non-platformed environment, they would have to file multiple tickets across disconnected infrastructure departments and resort to copying and pasting insecure YAML manifests from legacy repositories, delaying deployment by weeks.

patternViews.name: Self-Service Portal Task
patternViews.description: Utilizing Backstage to trigger the automated creation of the required environment and abstract away the infrastructure details.

narrativeContexts.context: The developer navigates directly to the Internal Developer Portal (Backstage) and selects the standard Java Spring Boot scaffolding template designed by the DevEx team.
By simply providing the target Git repository URL, the developer initiates the Golden Path, offloading the heavy configuration burden entirely to the platform's automated logic.

patternViews.name: Automated Scaffolding Action
patternViews.description: The platform engine leverages Shipwright, Cloud Native Buildpacks, and GitOps to autonomously deploy the asset.

narrativeContexts.context: The portal automatically generates the repository, linking it to a robust CI pipeline that compiles the code and builds a secure OCI image via Cloud Native Buildpacks (Shipwright).
Crucially, comprehensive observability endpoints and declarative HTTPRoute definitions are dynamically injected into the deployment manifests, baking in best practices without manual intervention.

patternViews.name: Velocity Increase Result
patternViews.description: The service is live, strictly secure-by-default, and organizational DORA metrics improve exponentially.

narrativeContexts.context: An intelligent GitOps controller residing securely inside the cluster detects the new manifests and autonomously synchronizes the live cluster state with the Git repository.

As a direct result, the developer’s "Time to First Service" drops precipitously from weeks to minutes. Cognitive load is effectively eliminated, and organizational DORA metrics—specifically Deployment Frequency and Lead Time—increase dramatically.

narratives.description: The strategic rationale for abandoning proprietary PaaS in favor of upstream CNCF architectures.

narrativeContexts.context: As organizations mature in their cloud-native journey, the need for hyper-customized developer experiences frequently drive architecture teams to consider open source solutions.

Constructing a bespoke Internal Developer Platform (IDP) from the upstream Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) ecosystem requires replicating the cohesive, frictionless developer experience of comprehensive commercial platforms while maintaining the unparalleled flexibility of raw Kubernetes.

This endeavor fundamentally shifts the "integration tax"—the cost and effort of ensuring distinct software components interoperate smoothly—from commercial vendors directly to the internal platform engineering organization. The success of such an initiative relies not merely on adopting community projects, but on a holistic socio-technical transformation.

The ultimate objective is to architect an ecosystem that dramatically reduces cognitive load for application developers, enforces complex security requirements inherently, and operates with the reliability, availability, and ease of use of a premier commercial product.

description: This coordinating macro-practice orchestrates the entire Ansible Automation Platform 2.6 adoption lifecycle. It explicitly does not define new Alphas, Activities, or discrete Work Products. name: AAP 2.6 Automation Mesh Operations Practice
description: This practice operationalizes the powerful Automation Mesh capabilities of AAP 2.6. It focuses entirely on the technical design, TLS configuration, and deployment of distributed Hop nodes and Execution nodes. The practice aims to securely route automation traffic out from the centralized control plane across varied, often highly isolated enterprise network perimeters and DMZs.
authors: Generated by Claude from source methodology

narratives.name: Mesh Practice Overview
narratives.narrativeName: Scaling Execution with the Automation Mesh
narratives.description: Overcoming network latency and security boundaries

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise networks frequently feature disjointed perimeters, strict firewalls, and distant geographical datacenters. Relying on the central Automation Controller to execute SSH commands across the globe introduces unacceptable latency and often violates strict security policies regarding inbound connections.

The Automation Mesh solves this by providing a dedicated overlay network utilizing the Receptor protocol. This architecture enables the explicit separation of the control plane from the execution plane.

By deploying Hop nodes (which route traffic but do not execute code) at network boundaries, and Execution nodes (which run user-space jobs locally via ansible-runner with Podman isolation) deep within the target datacenters, organizations can securely proxy automation instructions. This practice codifies the configuration of these nodes, ensuring TLS peering is established and jobs are routed efficiently without requiring direct SSH access from the central controllers.

alphas.name: Automation Mesh
alphas.description: The distributed overlay network of Control nodes, routing Hop nodes, and localized Execution nodes that manage workload distribution across complex topographies.

narratives.name: Mesh Context
narratives.description: Solving severe network latency and strict perimeter boundary issues

narrativeContexts.context: Automation mesh fundamentally enables the physical and logical separation of the control plane from the execution plane. When target enterprise hosts are located deep behind nested firewalls, hop nodes deployed in DMZs act essentially like intelligent jump hosts.

These hop nodes securely route Receptor protocol traffic (specifically over TCP port 27199) directly to the execution nodes. Crucially, the execution nodes utilize Podman container isolation to spin up execution environments and run the actual playbooks locally near the target infrastructure, virtually eliminating latency and avoiding massive firewall hole-punching.

narrativeContexts.context: Without an explicit, code-driven definition of how nodes connect, an automation mesh can quickly become a fragmented, disconnected set of stranded servers.
The configuration file dictates exactly which nodes listen for connections and which nodes initiate them, establishing the exact path that execution instructions will traverse.

narrativeContexts.context: To automate servers located in a highly isolated, highly secured DMZ, network engineers deploy a Hop node in the DMZ perimeter and an Execution node inside the DMZ payload zone.
They carefully configure the inventory variable peers to explicitly link the central Control plane to the Hop node, and subsequently link the Hop node down to the Execution node.

narratives.description: Verifying the mesh architecture functions under load

narrativeContexts.context: The mesh nodes are installed and show as 'Ready' in the UI;
But visual status alone does not guarantee that complex routing hops will successfully transfer execution environment images and playbook payloads over constrained links;

Therefore, engineers execute explicit validation playbooks assigned to edge Instance Groups, monitoring the Receptor logs to ensure the payload is routed efficiently and executes locally on the remote podman instance.

name: AAP 2.6 Governance and Access Practice
description: This practice operationalizes the critical day-2 governance configurations necessary to secure the platform. It specifically governs the setup of the unified Platform Gateway, the integration of enterprise Identity Providers (IdP), and the meticulous mapping of Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to Organizations and Teams, leveraging Configuration as Code to enforce strict security postures.
authors: Generated by Claude from source methodology

narratives.name: Governance Practice Overview
narratives.description: Managing the Day-2 operations for organizational scale

narrativeContexts.context: Once the infrastructure is successfully installed and verified, the platform must be aggressively secured and logically partitioned before users are onboarded. AAP 2.6 revolutionizes this by centralizing all component authentication entirely through the new Platform Gateway.
This architectural shift eliminates the disjointed legacy process of managing users separately within the Automation Controller, Automation Hub, and Event-Driven Ansible instances.

By utilizing the ansible.platform collection, administrators can natively build code-driven pipelines that automatically deploy Organizations, define granular Teams, map SSO attributes, and assign highly specific Custom Roles (via the new DAB RBAC engine) directly through the Gateway API. This ensures real-time synchronization of permissions across all platform services, completely bypassing the known 15-minute synchronization delays inherent to legacy automation controller APIs.

alphas.name: Role-Based Access Control
alphas.description: The comprehensive governance framework that maps authenticated users to hierarchical organizational roles, dictating explicit permissions across all platform resources.

narratives.name: RBAC Context
narratives.narrativeName: The Power of Unified Gateway Access
narratives.description: The organizational shift to centralized authentication logic

narrativeContexts.context: AAP 2.6 integrates the entirety of its RBAC model deeply into the Platform Gateway. System Administrators are empowered to define macro Organizations, nest Teams within them, and grant highly granular execution or viewing permissions to specific automation resources (like job templates or credentials).

Managing this access exclusively via the Unified UI or the new Platform Gateway API is now a strict operational mandate. It ensures immediate, real-time synchronization across all platform components. Continuing to utilize legacy automation controller APIs causes propagation delays of up to 15 minutes, which frequently results in sudden authentication errors when users attempt to interact with the Event-Driven Ansible controller.

A major enhancement in version 2.6, driven by the Django-ansible-base (DAB) RBAC capabilities, is the ability to construct Custom Roles natively via the /api/v2/role_definitions/ endpoint. This allows administrators to delegate precise resource creation permissions (e.g., allowing a developer to create a project but not execute it) rather than relying on blunt, predefined system roles.

narratives.description: The rationale for entirely avoiding manual UI configuration

narrativeContexts.context: While the Unified UI is powerful, manually clicking through web forms to configure dozens of roles, teams, and users is inherently unscalable and highly prone to configuration drift over time.

Utilizing the newly consolidated ansible.platform collection to manage all RBAC settings ensures a reproducible, highly consistent security foundation. It allows the security posture to be reviewed in Git pull requests before being applied to the Gateway via automation pipelines.

name: AAP 2.6 Containerized Deployment Practice
description: This practice operationalizes the physical installation of the platform on Red Hat Enterprise Linux. It focuses explicitly on managing the transition to rootless, podman-based containerized deployments, meticulously managing the strict inventory variables required by the installation bundle, and executing rigorous host system preparation before the installer playbooks are triggered.
authors: Generated by Claude from source methodology

narratives.name: Deployment Practice Overview
narratives.description: Understanding the operational shift to a container-first deployment model

narrativeContexts.context: With the release of version 2.6, Red Hat enforces a strategic container-first model, actively deprecating the legacy RPM-based installers in preparation for their complete removal in subsequent versions.

The Containerized AAP model utilizes Podman to run the platform in rootless containers on RHEL hosts. This drastically enhances system security while seamlessly isolating the complex product lifecycle from the underlying operating system lifecycle.

This practice codifies the highly rigorous prerequisites necessary to execute this new methodology. It dictates the establishment of dedicated non-root users with specific sudo privileges, the configuration of offline or online Red Hat registry access, and the meticulous parameterization of the inventory variables required to execute the ansible.containerized_installer.install playbook flawlessly.

alphas.name: Installation Configuration
alphas.description: The comprehensive state of the host environments, network access, and parameterized settings required to successfully execute the containerized platform installer.

narratives.name: Installation Configuration Context
narratives.description: The critical importance of exhaustive system preparation

narrativeContexts.context: The containerized installer relies absolutely on a meticulously constructed inventory file. This file acts as the singular source of truth, dictating all passwords, database hosts, integration points, and feature flags (such as hub_admin_password, gateway_pg_host, and specific NGINX TLS paths).

Before any execution can occur, the host nodes themselves must be explicitly prepared. This involves installing required packages like ansible-core and podman, configuring NTP clients to prevent clock drift, and establishing a Red Hat registry service account to authenticate online container image pulls from registry.redhat.io.

narratives.name: Inventory File Purpose
narratives.description: Why the inventory file serves as the absolute source of truth

narrativeContexts.context: Unlike legacy enterprise software requiring manual GUI-driven setups, AAP 2.6 is deployed via Ansible automation itself. The inventory file contains structural host groups (e.g., [automationhub], [execution_nodes]) and massive dictionaries of specialized variables.

narratives.description: The rationale behind OS-level prerequisites

narrativeContexts.context: We need to deploy the containerized automation platform securely and efficiently across multiple nodes;
But running containers as the root user presents an unacceptable security vulnerability in highly regulated enterprise environments;

Therefore, we explicitly provision a dedicated admin user with sudo privileges, install the ansible-core packages, and ensure the deployment framework utilizes rootless Podman containers to strictly isolate the execution environment.

narrativeContexts.context: Platform engineers painstakingly populate the inventory file with specific variables derived directly from the logical models created during the Architecture phase.

This complex task involves mapping container-specific variables like hub_pg_database or automationhub_nginx_tls_files_remote, setting up the exact registry authentication logic, and ensuring the [all:vars] section correctly dictates the overarching platform behavior. narrativeContexts.context: The IT operations team consistently struggled with severe configuration drift and inconsistent platform deployments across their isolated development, staging, and production environments, leading to unpredictable downtime.

name: AAP 2.6 Foundation Architecture Practice
description: This practice establishes the core architectural blueprints and topological decisions required before any physical infrastructure is provisioned. It focuses specifically on evaluating organizational capacity against the opinionated deployment models tested by Red Hat, explicitly mapping the required components to stringent system requirements, and planning the integration of external databases and network ports to ensure long-term scalability.

narratives.name: Architecture Practice Overview
narratives.description: The necessity of upfront topological and capacity planning

narrativeContexts.context: Successful platform adoption requires rigorous upfront capacity planning to select the correct infrastructure shape. The platform offers opinionated, tested topologies designed specifically to prevent performance misconfiguration and ensure future scalability.

Organizations must deliberately choose between a 'Growth' topology—an all-in-one consolidated approach suited for smaller footprints and initial adoption—and an 'Enterprise' topology, which provides true high availability and redundancy necessary for massive volumes of concurrent automation execution.

This practice codifies the architectural decision-making process, ensuring that storage constraints, network port allocations, database connection limits, and critical component integrations are modeled logically before the containerized installation bundle is ever executed by the engineering teams.

alphas.name: Deployment Topology
alphas.description: The overarching structural design of the platform environment, dictating node allocation, service redundancy, and scaling constraints based on organizational workload.

narratives.name: Topology Selection Context
narratives.description: Understanding the technical constraints and benefits of distinct topological shapes

narrativeContexts.context: Red Hat explicitly tests specific system configurations to ensure maximum uptime and consistent performance. The Container Growth topology represents an all-in-one deployment model, demanding a minimum baseline of 16 GB RAM and 4 CPUs, though 32 GB is strictly required if collections are seeded during installation.

Conversely, the Container Enterprise topology scales the core components out to multiple independent nodes. This advanced configuration necessitates external load balancing infrastructure (such as HAProxy or an external NGINX appliance) and often mandates customer-provided external PostgreSQL databases to effectively bypass the restrictive 100-connection limit inherent to basic operator-deployed databases.

Failure to accurately project the 30-day database storage limits (which can quickly exceed 100 GB depending on job frequency and playbook output) or concurrent job capacity will lead directly to architectural bottlenecks.

name: Ansible Automation Platform 2.6 Enterprise Lifecycle Method
description: This overarching method orchestrates the planning, deployment, and operationalization of Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform 2.6. It guides enterprise platform engineering teams through the transition from legacy automation scripts or older RPM-based environments to a modernized, container-first architecture. The method unifies the deployment of core components and coordinates the establishment of secure, distributed execution layers via the Automation Mesh. By composing these capabilities into a structured progression, the method ensures organizations can build a reproducible, secure, and scalable automation foundation capable of handling enterprise workloads.

narratives.name: Strategic Method Intent
narratives.narrativeName: The Transition to Containerized Enterprise Automation
narratives.description: The overarching strategic rationale for adopting the AAP 2.6 methodology

narrativeContexts.context: As enterprise organizations scale their automation initiatives beyond isolated scripts and departmental use cases, the need for a highly resilient, standardized, and horizontally scalable architecture becomes a critical operational requirement. Previous deployment models often struggled with underlying operating system dependency management and complex upgrade friction.

The Ansible Automation Platform 2.6 methodology addresses these challenges by enforcing a strategic architectural shift toward a container-first approach. It utilizes Podman to execute the platform within rootless containers directly on Red Hat Enterprise Linux host machines, thereby enhancing security and cleanly isolating the product lifecycle from the underlying infrastructure lifecycle.

Furthermore, the introduction of the Platform Gateway provides a unified graphical interface and a centralized authentication service, entirely replacing the fragmented access models of previous platform versions. This method operationalizes these significant architectural shifts into a cohesive, step-by-step organizational adoption journey, ensuring teams can standardize practices, operate reliably in production, and prepare for massive scale.

practices.name: AAP 2.6 Governance and Access Practice
practices.description: This practice operationalizes the critical day-2 governance configurations necessary to secure the platform. It specifically governs the setup of the unified Platform Gateway, the integration of enterprise Identity Providers (IdP), and the meticulous mapping of Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to Organizations and Teams, leveraging Configuration as Code to enforce strict security postures.
authors: Generated by Claude from source methodology

narratives.name: Governance Practice Overview
narratives.description: Managing the Day-2 operations for organizational scale

narrativeContexts.context: Once the infrastructure is successfully installed and verified, the platform must be aggressively secured and logically partitioned before users are onboarded. AAP 2.6 revolutionizes this by centralizing all component authentication entirely through the new Platform Gateway.
This architectural shift eliminates the disjointed legacy process of managing users separately within the Automation Controller, Automation Hub, and Event-Driven Ansible instances.

By utilizing the ansible.platform collection, administrators can natively build code-driven pipelines that automatically deploy Organizations, define granular Teams, map SSO attributes, and assign highly specific Custom Roles (via the new DAB RBAC engine) directly through the Gateway API. This ensures real-time synchronization of permissions across all platform services, completely bypassing the known 15-minute synchronization delays inherent to legacy automation controller APIs.

narratives.name: RBAC Context
narratives.narrativeName: The Power of Unified Gateway Access
narratives.description: The organizational shift to centralized authentication logic

narrativeContexts.context: AAP 2.6 integrates the entirety of its RBAC model deeply into the Platform Gateway. System Administrators are empowered to define macro Organizations, nest Teams within them, and grant highly granular execution or viewing permissions to specific automation resources (like job templates or credentials).

Managing this access exclusively via the Unified UI or the new Platform Gateway API is now a strict operational mandate. It ensures immediate, real-time synchronization across all platform components. Continuing to utilize legacy automation controller APIs causes propagation delays of up to 15 minutes, which frequently results in sudden authentication errors when users attempt to interact with the Event-Driven Ansible controller.

A major enhancement in version 2.6, driven by the Django-ansible-base (DAB) RBAC capabilities, is the ability to construct Custom Roles natively via the /api/v2/role_definitions/ endpoint. This allows administrators to delegate precise resource creation permissions (e.g., allowing a developer to create a project but not execute it) rather than relying on blunt, predefined system roles.

practices.name: AAP 2.6 Automation Mesh Operations Practice
practices.description: This practice operationalizes the powerful Automation Mesh capabilities of AAP 2.6. It focuses entirely on the technical design, TLS configuration, and deployment of distributed Hop nodes and Execution nodes. The practice aims to securely route automation traffic out from the centralized control plane across varied, often highly isolated enterprise network perimeters and DMZs.
authors: Generated by Claude from source methodology

narratives.name: Mesh Practice Overview
narratives.narrativeName: Scaling Execution with the Automation Mesh
narratives.description: Overcoming network latency and security boundaries

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise networks frequently feature disjointed perimeters, strict firewalls, and distant geographical datacenters. Relying on the central Automation Controller to execute SSH commands across the globe introduces unacceptable latency and often violates strict security policies regarding inbound connections.

The Automation Mesh solves this by providing a dedicated overlay network utilizing the Receptor protocol. This architecture enables the explicit separation of the control plane from the execution plane.

By deploying Hop nodes (which route traffic but do not execute code) at network boundaries, and Execution nodes (which run user-space jobs locally via ansible-runner with Podman isolation) deep within the target datacenters, organizations can securely proxy automation instructions. This practice codifies the configuration of these nodes, ensuring TLS peering is established and jobs are routed efficiently without requiring direct SSH access from the central controllers.

alphas.name: Automation Mesh
alphas.description: The distributed overlay network of Control nodes, routing Hop nodes, and localized Execution nodes that manage workload distribution across complex topographies.

narratives.name: Mesh Context
narratives.description: Solving severe network latency and strict perimeter boundary issues

narrativeContexts.context: Automation mesh fundamentally enables the physical and logical separation of the control plane from the execution plane. When target enterprise hosts are located deep behind nested firewalls, hop nodes deployed in DMZs act essentially like intelligent jump hosts.

These hop nodes securely route Receptor protocol traffic (specifically over TCP port 27199) directly to the execution nodes. Crucially, the execution nodes utilize Podman container isolation to spin up execution environments and run the actual playbooks locally near the target infrastructure, virtually eliminating latency and avoiding massive firewall hole-punching.

The configuration file dictates exactly which nodes listen for connections and which nodes initiate them, establishing the exact path that execution instructions will traverse.

practices.name: AAP 2.6 Lifecycle Orchestration Practice
practices.description: This coordinating macro-practice orchestrates the entire Ansible Automation Platform 2.6 adoption lifecycle. It explicitly does not define new Alphas, Activities, or discrete Work Products. Instead, it establishes an overarching temporal framework—via comprehensive Patterns—that accurately tracks the simultaneous progression of architectural planning, containerized physical deployment, access governance, and mesh scaling across unified organizational delivery phases.

narratives.name: Orchestration Overview
narratives.description: How the four disparate practices compose into a single unified lifecycle

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise platform engineering simply cannot occur in isolated silos. High-level architecture must seamlessly inform infrastructure provisioning, which must be physically verified before complex governance policies and distributed mesh networks can be applied safely.

This Lifecycle pattern coordinates these distinct capability domains, ensuring that organizations achieve operational maturity sequentially and logically. For example, the Deployment Topology must reach the Baselined state before the Installation Configuration is permitted to enter the Executed state, explicitly preventing costly deployment rework.

By observing the Pattern View Matrix, technology leaders can track the holistic health of the automation rollout, ensuring that security (RBAC) and scale (Mesh) mature in lockstep with the core infrastructure platform.

activitySpaces.name: Monitor Value Realization
activitySpaces.description: Track KPIs such as deployment frequency, MTTR, and developer adoption rates to proactively manage bottlenecks and prove continuous ROI.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Platform Economics
activitySpaces.description: Define chargeback/showback models, right-size infrastructure, optimize costs through FinOps practices, and transition from CapEx to OpEx.

activitySpaces.description: Conduct user research, utilize Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks, and ensure the platform demonstrates value through product management practices.
